analysis.one_liner: Forces large profitable public companies that buy back their own stock to pay employees an equal cash dividend.
analysis.headline: The Worker Dividend Act was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 6, 2018, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any publicly traded company with more than $250 million in U.S. earnings that buys back its own stock to also pay every U.S. employee an equal cash "worker dividend." The dividend would equal the lesser of what the company spent on buybacks or half its U.S. earnings above $250 million, and companies that refused would owe a tax of the same amount instead.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. employees of large, profitable publicly traded companies — including full-time and part-time workers, who would each receive an equal cash payment on top of their regular pay whenever the company repurchases its own stock. At big companies that spend billions on buybacks, that could mean thousands of dollars per worker per year.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large, profitable public companies

how_it_helps.text: When a covered company repurchases its own stock, it must pay U.S. employees a dividend equal to the lesser of its buyback spending or 50% of U.S. earnings above $250 million, spread equally among all employees.
The payment must come on top of — not instead of — the compensation the employee would ordinarily receive, so companies cannot shift existing pay to claim compliance.
Part-time employees are included, with pro rata payments based on hours worked, and payments are due within 60 days of the end of the tax year.
Companies that fail to pay the dividend owe an excise tax equal to the required dividend, giving them a direct financial stake in sharing buyback wealth with workers.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies with over $250 million in U.S. earnings that buy back their own stock: they either pay the worker dividend or owe the government a tax of the same amount. Shareholders bear the indirect cost, since money that would fund buybacks goes to workers or to the Treasury instead.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large public companies and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies only to open-market stock repurchases, so companies could simply switch to paying dividends or making other shareholder payouts to avoid it — legally enriching shareholders while workers get nothing.

The bill lets employers convert the dividend into documented 'increases in regular compensation,' a flexibility that the bill itself acknowledges could be abused by requiring regulations 'to prevent avoidance' of the substitution rules.
The tax raises no revenue if companies comply — it is a mandate, not a funding source — and companies would face new reporting and compliance costs to the Treasury, the SEC, and the Labor Department.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers at profitable public companies could be substantial — buybacks by large U.S. firms run into the billions, and the bill would force an equal amount to flow to employees rather than only to shareholders. The main weakness is the design: because the trigger is only open-market buybacks, companies can restructure their shareholder payouts to sidestep the requirement, so the guarantee is strong in form but potentially porous in practice. It also puts a new compliance burden on affected companies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the 115th Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Worker Dividend Act on March 6, 2018, joined by one cosponsor, Senator Robert Casey.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded: the Finance Committee took no markup and the Senate never voted, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large profitable public companies that repurchase their own stock are better off, since they never faced a requirement to split buyback money with employees or pay an equal tax, and shareholders continue to receive the full benefit of buybacks.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; both sponsors were Democrats and the bill sat untouched in the Republican-chaired Senate Finance Committee.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations that buy back their own stock
industries.note: The bill would force any large profitable public company that repurchases its own stock to hand an equal sum to U.S. employees or pay it to the Treasury as a tax. Companies currently direct buyback money exclusively to shareholders, so the bill directly redistributes that payout to workers.

Shareholders benefit from buybacks, which raise stock prices by reducing the share count; the bill would shrink or make buybacks more expensive, and companies might switch to dividends instead. Asset managers with large index holdings would see those payout strategies curtailed.
